# 5. Results

This section reports what the estimation produced, in the order the exhibits present it. Table 6 carries the specification diagnostics and the input elasticities. Figure 1 disaggregates the service comparison by the four sources of provision. Figure 2 follows the comparison across survey rounds, Figure 3 across the content of the services provided, and Figures 4 and 5 across farmer characteristics, crops and regions. Tables S7 and S8 hold the full frontier and the inefficiency function; Table S5, Table S6 and Figure S1 hold the balance evidence behind the matched sample.

One convention governs every number below. A difference is reported as the served group minus the unserved group, so a positive value means farms in communities with an agricultural service source do better on that measure. The three measures are not interchangeable. The technology gap ratio describes the frontier a group can reach, technical efficiency describes how close a farmer gets to that frontier, and meta-technical efficiency is their product. A group can be worse on the first and better on the second, and the sign of the third then depends on which effect is larger.

## 5.1 Diagnostic tests

Two specification choices are settled by test rather than assumption. A likelihood-ratio test rejects the Cobb-Douglas restriction against the translog on the naive national frontier (LR = `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$functional_form$naive$lr), 1)`, `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$functional_form$naive$df), 0)` degrees of freedom) and on each group frontier separately (LR = `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$functional_form$none$lr), 1)` for the unserved group, `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$functional_form$any$lr), 1)` for the served group), all three below the 0.001 level. A second likelihood-ratio test, of a single common frontier against the two group-specific frontiers, returns `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "Meta frontier LR test", "meta_m"), 0)` on the matched sample and `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "Meta frontier LR test", "meta_u"), 0)` on the unmatched sample. Served and unserved communities do not share a technology, which is the condition the meta-frontier framework requires.

The theoretical properties are the weaker part of the specification and we report them plainly. After imposing monotonicity and evaluating quasi-concavity, monotonicity holds for `r fmt_num(100 * assert_present(objs$diagnostics$mono$none), 2)` percent of observations under the unserved frontier, `r fmt_num(100 * assert_present(objs$diagnostics$mono$naive), 2)` percent under the naive national frontier, and `r fmt_num(100 * assert_present(objs$diagnostics$mono$meta_m), 2)` percent under the matched meta-frontier. Under the served frontier it holds for `r fmt_num(100 * assert_present(objs$diagnostics$mono$any), 2)` percent, the lowest rate in the set. Curvature is satisfied less often everywhere, at `r fmt_num(100 * assert_present(objs$diagnostics$curv$none), 2)` percent, `r fmt_num(100 * assert_present(objs$diagnostics$curv$any), 2)` percent and `r fmt_num(100 * assert_present(objs$diagnostics$curv$naive), 2)` percent for the three single-technology frontiers and `r fmt_num(100 * assert_present(objs$diagnostics$curv$meta_m), 2)` percent for the matched meta-frontier. The served-group frontier is thus the least well behaved of the four, and every estimate reported below that involves it inherits that weakness.

Three tests of one-sided error support the frontier structure. On the naive national frontier the residual skewness statistic is `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "Schmidt & Lin (1984) a", "naive"), 3)`, the third-moment statistic `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "Coelli (1995) a", "naive"), 3)`, and the likelihood ratio for the presence of inefficiency `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "Gutierrez (2001) a", "naive"), 3)`. Each rejects its null, and each rejects again on both group frontiers. The share of output variance attributable to inefficiency rather than noise is `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$diagnostics$gamma$none), 3)` for the unserved group and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$diagnostics$gamma$any), 3)` for the served group, rising to `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$diagnostics$gamma$meta), 3)` on the matched meta-frontier.

## 5.2 Output elasticities

Every input contributes positively to output on every frontier, and all estimates in the elasticity block of Table 6 are significant at the 1 percent level. Land dominates. Its elasticity is `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$land$none), 3)` on the unserved frontier and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$land$any), 3)` on the served frontier, roughly four times the next largest input. Family labour follows at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$family_labour$none), 3)` and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$family_labour$any), 3)`, then planting material, hired labour, pesticide and fertilizer, each of them an order of magnitude below land. Returns to scale are close to constant in both groups, at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$rts$none), 3)` for the unserved group and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$rts$any), 3)` for the served group.

The two frontiers do not weight their inputs identically, and the differences are small but systematic. The served group draws more from land, by `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$land$gapm), 3)`, and more from hired labour, fertilizer and pesticide, by `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$hired_labour$gapm), 3)`, `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$fertilizer$gapm), 3)` and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$pesticide$gapm), 3)`. The unserved group draws more from planting material and family labour, where the differences run the other way at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$planting_materials$gapm), 3)` and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$family_labour$gapm), 3)`. All six are stored matched-sample differences and all six are significant at the 1 percent level. The difference in returns to scale, `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$rts$gapm), 3)`, is the only estimate in the entire elasticity block that is not statistically distinguishable from zero. Whatever separates these two technologies, it is not scale.

## 5.3 Technology adoption and technical efficiency

The aggregate comparison runs in two directions at once. Farms in served communities sit on a frontier substantially further below the meta-frontier than farms in unserved communities: the technology gap ratio is `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$tgr$none), 3)` without services and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$tgr$any), 3)` with them, a difference of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$tgr$gap), 3)`. On the same matched sample they use that frontier better, with technical efficiency of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$te$any), 3)` against `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$te$none), 3)`, a difference of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$te$gap), 3)`. Both are significant at the 1 percent level. Both are large beside anything reported in Section 2, where no unadjusted difference between the two groups approached this magnitude.

Net of each other, almost nothing remains. Meta-technical efficiency is `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$mte$none), 3)` for the unserved group and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$mte$any), 3)` for the served group. That difference, `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$mte$gap), 3)` or `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$mte$gap_pct), 2)` percent, is significant at the 1 percent level and roughly an order of magnitude smaller than either of the two differences producing it. The overall measure is therefore the least informative of the three here, not the most: it is small because two large effects nearly cancel, and it is the same size as it would be if neither effect existed.

The four sources of provision do not behave alike, and Figure 1 is where that shows. Active extension reproduces the aggregate pattern almost exactly, with a technology gap difference of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services3$tgr$gap), 3)`, an efficiency difference of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services3$te$gap), 3)`, and a net difference of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services3$mte$gap), 3)`, all three significant at the 1 percent level. Of the three sources it is the only one whose components both move in the direction the aggregate implies, and its net result is the largest positive of the three.

Agricultural and fishing associations show the same two directions at close to three times the magnitude. The technology gap difference is `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services1$tgr$gap), 3)` against the aggregate's `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$tgr$gap), 3)`, and the efficiency difference `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services1$te$gap), 3)` against `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$te$gap), 3)`. At that scale the offset no longer holds, and the net difference is negative at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services1$mte$gap), 3)`. Cooperatives are the opposite case. Neither the technology gap difference of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services2$tgr$gap), 3)` nor the efficiency difference of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services2$te$gap), 3)` is statistically distinguishable from zero, yet their product is, at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services2$mte$gap), 3)` and significant at the 1 percent level. Three sources, three routes, and net results that differ in sign.

Figure 2 follows the comparison round by round, and the technology gap closes across the period. The difference is `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$tgr$gap$GLSS5), 3)` in 2005/06, `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$tgr$gap$GLSS6), 3)` in 2012/13 and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$tgr$gap$GLSS7), 3)` in 2016/17. The first two are significant at the 1 percent level; the last is the only estimate in the entire series that is not distinguishable from zero. By the most recent round the frontier available to served communities is statistically indistinguishable from the frontier available to unserved ones. The efficiency difference shows no comparable movement, staying positive and significant in every round at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$te$gap$GLSS5), 3)`, `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$te$gap$GLSS6), 3)` and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$te$gap$GLSS7), 3)`.

Because one component moves and the other does not, their product changes sign. Overall performance in served communities sits `r fmt_num(abs(assert_present(objs$by_wave$mte$gap$GLSS5)), 3)` below unserved communities in 2005/06, `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$mte$gap$GLSS6), 3)` above them in 2012/13, and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$mte$gap$GLSS7), 3)` above them in 2016/17, each estimate significant at the 1 percent level. The pooled difference of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$mte$gap), 3)` reported above is an average taken across a comparison that reverses direction inside the period, and no single round in the data produces it.

## 5.4 Robustness of main findings

The estimates above are properties of the matched sample, and Table 6 reports both samples so that the contribution of matching can be read directly. Without matching the technology gap difference is `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "te/TGR/Unmatched", "diff"), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "te/TGR/Matched", "diff"), 3)`, and the efficiency difference `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "te/TE/Unmatched", "diff"), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "te/TE/Matched", "diff"), 3)`; both components are understated. The net measure moves further than either. Meta-technical efficiency differs by `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "te/MTE/Unmatched", "diff"), 3)` unmatched and `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "te/MTE/Matched", "diff"), 3)` matched, which is a change of sign rather than of magnitude. Section 2.2 showed that the two groups differ on characteristics that independently predict performance, and this is what those differences are worth once removed.

Specification checks appear in Figure S2, which re-estimates the aggregate comparison under alternative functional forms, alternative inefficiency distributions and alternative matching metrics. Section 4.3 has already noted that the two best-balanced distance metrics differ only in the fourth decimal of the selection criterion, so the choice between them is not a source of variation. The naive national frontier gives one further reference point: it puts technical efficiency at `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "te/TE/Matched", "naive"), 3)` on the matched sample, between the two group-specific values, which is what a single pooled technology should produce when it averages over two.

## 5.5 Observed heterogeneity

Figure 3 disaggregates the comparison by the content of the services a community provides. Four of the eight service types support an estimate on the served side, and among those four the net differences span more than half a point: post-harvest and marketing support at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_post_harvest$provided$mte), 3)`, planting and seed-use advice at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_planting$provided$mte), 3)`, agrochemical support at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_agchemicals$provided$mte), 3)`, and mechanization at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_mechanization$provided$mte), 3)`. Section 2.1 explains why the other four service types cannot be estimated on the served side.

Decomposed, that spread sits almost entirely in one component. The technology gap difference is negative for all four and varies little across them, from `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_post_harvest$provided$tgr), 3)` for post-harvest support to `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_mechanization$provided$tgr), 3)` for mechanization. The efficiency difference varies enormously, from `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_post_harvest$provided$te), 3)` for post-harvest support to `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_mechanization$provided$te), 3)` for mechanization, with planting advice at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_planting$provided$te), 3)` and agrochemical support at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_agchemicals$provided$te), 3)` in between. What a community's service menu contains bears on how well farmers use the frontier available to them, and very little on which frontier that is.

Figures 4 and 5 disaggregate by farmer characteristics, crop and region. The technology gap difference is negative for both men and women and larger in absolute terms for women, at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$heterogeneity$female[["1"]]$tgr), 3)` against `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$heterogeneity$female[["0"]]$tgr), 3)`, while the efficiency difference is positive for both. Net of the two, overall performance is lower in served communities for both and more so for women, at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$heterogeneity$female[["1"]]$mte), 3)` against `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$heterogeneity$female[["0"]]$mte), 3)`. Across age categories the net difference rises with age and turns positive only in the oldest, reaching `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$heterogeneity$age[["3"]]$mte), 3)` against `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$heterogeneity$age[["1"]]$mte), 3)` in the youngest. By crop it is positive for rice (`r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$heterogeneity$crop$Rice$mte), 3)`), pepper (`r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$heterogeneity$crop$Pepper$mte), 3)`) and yam, and negative for cassava (`r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$heterogeneity$crop$Cassava$mte), 3)`), maize and cocoa. Expressed as a percentage of the unserved group's score, the crop ordering runs from `r assert_present(objs$ranked$crop$level[[1]])` at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$ranked$crop$pct[[1]]), 2)` percent to `r assert_present(objs$ranked$crop$level[[length(objs$ranked$crop$level)]])` at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$ranked$crop$pct[[length(objs$ranked$crop$pct)]]), 2)` percent, and the regional ordering from `r assert_present(objs$ranked$region$level[[1]])` at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$ranked$region$pct[[1]]), 2)` percent to `r assert_present(objs$ranked$region$level[[length(objs$ranked$region$level)]])` at `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$ranked$region$pct[[length(objs$ranked$region$pct)]]), 2)` percent.

One feature of the regional disaggregation is a property of the sample rather than a result, and we flag it here rather than leave it to be read as a finding. In Northern, Upper East and Upper West, and correspondingly in the Guinea and Sudan Savanah zones, the efficiency difference is estimated at exactly zero and the technology gap difference at under one percentage point in absolute value. Those are the strata in which service provision is close to universal, so the within-stratum comparison has very few unserved farms to draw on. The estimates for the three northern regions and the two savanah zones should be read as uninformative rather than as evidence that agricultural services make no difference there.
